paper_title: Speculative Sampling in Interactive Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Interactive video generation commonly relies on small bidirectional chunks to reduce response latency. Yet our preliminary experiments show that larger chunks improve video quality and better utilize GPU parallelism, allowing more latents to be sampled with only a modest increase in sampling time. Motivated by these observations, we propose Speculative Sampling, a strategy that combines the modeling power of large bidirectional windows with the low-latency interaction of small ones. It expands the modeling window by appending noise latents as padding and caches the resulting predictions for reuse when the condition remains unchanged. Predictions are delivered incrementally, while the uncommitted future remains replaceable. Our latency analysis shows that this removes the waiting-time lower bound imposed by chunk boundaries, shifting the optimization focus from reducing chunk size to accelerating per-chunk sampling. Bidirectional window size thus becomes a decision variable for jointly optimizing visual quality and sampling time, rather than a necessary constraint on low-latency interaction. This opens a path to serving large bidirectional models in interactive streaming systems without complex streaming post-training.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Interactive video generation requires newly arriving conditions to influence ongoing playback promptly. viewer may change camera command or action instruction at any time, while existing video continues to play. Generation throughput alone does not capture this requirement: fast model can still leave the viewer waiting for generation or playback boundary. natural route is fine-grained autoregressive generation. Advances in rollout training and few-step distillation have made this route increasingly practical (Huang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025). Smaller generation chunks provide more frequent opportunities to incorporate new conditions, enabling fine-grained interaction, but may limit joint temporal modeling and parallel efficiency. This raises our central question: must low-latency interaction come at the cost of smaller bidirectional modeling window? We introduce Speculative Sampling, strategy that combines the modeling power of large bidirectional windows with the low-latency interaction of small ones. It expands the modeling window with padding latents and caches their predictions for reuse when the condition remains unchanged, while allowing the predicted future to be revised when new conditions arrive (Figure 1). We first formulate serving model that separates condition arrivals, generation, output commitment, and playback. Generation is the computation needed for deliverable video output; for the latent diffusion models studied here, it includes DiT sampling and required VAE decoding. The model distinguishes generation time from phase-dependent random-arrival waiting imposed by scheduling and playback boundaries, and identifies replaceable outputs. When new output can enter playback only at chunk boundaries, the chunk duration imposes waiting floor even if generation is fast. We next examine chunk size K, the number of latent frames jointly sampled in one DiT sampling call. Changing affects joint temporal modeling and parallel efficiency, as well as the time needed cheneh@ustc.edu.cn 1 Figure 1: Fine-grained interaction without shrinking generation chunks. Our method preserves large-chunk joint sampling while allowing updates beyond the protected prefix, rather than only at chunk boundaries. Gray/green denote old/new conditions; the dashed line marks playback position at condition arrival, and thick green edges mark updated output. Positions represent video content, not computation time. to generate each chunk. Our chunk-size ablation shows higher aggregate video quality for largerchunk configurations than their frame-wise counterparts in the evaluated settings (Section 4). Larger chunks also better utilize GPU parallelism, allowing more latents to be sampled with only modest increase in sampling time. Together with the system model, this motivates retaining the benefits of joint generation while reducing the waiting imposed by coarse output commitment. Guided by the system model and chunk-size ablation, we develop our method to combine largechunk joint generation with fine-grained delivery. We expand the bidirectional modeling window by appending noise latents as padding. Rather than discarding the resulting predictions, we cache them for reuse when the condition remains unchanged, while keeping the uncommitted future replaceable. We formulate the controller as two-state finite-state machine that coordinates joint generation and incremental consumption of cached predictions, while playback continues independently. This decouples DiT sampling calls from individual deliveries: completed predictions are reused between condition updates, avoiding repeated sampling merely to support finer-grained delivery. The resulting design points to an alternative route to interactive video generation: shrinking chunks need not be prerequisite for low interaction latency. Instead, the optimization focus can shift to accelerating high-quality joint generation. DiT sampling acceleration and parallel acceleration can support this route. We further demonstrate this route by serving large bidirectional model in low-latency interactive streaming system without Self-Forcing-style post-training. Our contributions are fourfold: 1. simple serving-system model for interactive video generation. We formalize condition arrivals, generation, output commitment, and playback, distinguishing generation time from the additional waiting imposed by scheduling and playback boundaries (Section 3.1). 2. systematic analysis of chunk size. We study how chunk size affects video quality, generation time, and redundant computation, clarifying the trade-offs between joint modeling and responsiveness (Section 4; Appendices AB). 3. Recomputation-efficient speculative sampling. Guided by this model and analysis, we propose speculative sampling scheme formulated as two-state finite-state machine. It combines large-chunk joint generation with fine-grained output commitment, reusing predictions and replanning only feasible suffix when conditions change (Section 3). 4. An alternative route to interactive video generation. By separating chunk size from output commitment, we shift the optimization focus from shrinking chunks to accelerating high-quality joint generation, making per-chunk generation time central target for improving responsiveness.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Autoregressive video generation. Autoregressive video generation exploits temporal structure by predicting new content conditioned on the past (Yan et al., 2021). This provides natural interface for extending videos, including segment-wise continuation under changing prompts (Villegas et al., 2022). Bringing sequential prediction to diffusion models (Chen et al., 2024) leaves two practical challenges: the cost of repeated sampling and errors accumulated through generated history. Recent progress therefore targets efficient few-step causal generation (Yin et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026) and training aligned with self-generated, long-horizon rollouts (Huang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). Related rolling and bidirectional-window approaches retain joint temporal processing during sequential output (Kim et al., 2024; Kodaira et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Rui et al., 2026). NFD additionally describes speculative multi-frame sampling on frame-causal backbone to improve throughput, but retains causal mask within the enlarged window and therefore does not exploit bidirectional modeling across it (Cheng et al., 2025). Related control mechanisms include reuse or replanning of fully denoised futures with ground-truth observation feedback (Lillemark et al., 2026) and management of generationplayback lead (Bai et al., 2026). Our method studies complementary interface: retaining temporally bidirectional joint generation within each chunk while committing outputs at finer granularity under newly arriving conditions. Accelerating video generation. Acceleration targets several components of generation cost. Fewstep distillation (Yin et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026) and adversarial post-training (Lin et al., 2025) reduce DiT sampling steps. Pyramid Flow performs much of its DiT sampling below full spatial resolution and compresses history through temporal pyramid (Jin et al., 2024); FramePack reduces the historical-context token budget (Zhang et al., 2025a). FasterCache and TeaCache reuse intermediate computations across diffusion steps (Lv et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024), whereas Sliding Tile Attention and Sparse VideoGen reduce attention work through local or spatialtemporal sparsity (Zhang et al., 2025b; Xi et al., 2025). USP addresses distributed attention through sequence parallelism (Fang & Zhao, 2024). These methods have distinct training and inference requirements. Our perspective shifts the emphasis from shrinking generation chunks to accelerating their generation. By decoupling generation from output commitment, our method highlights per-chunk generation time, rather than chunk size alone, as key determinant of interaction latency. This places greater importance on accelerating joint generation instead of requiring increasingly fine-grained autoregressive models.

This would remove the need to shrink chunks or increase the models temporal frame rate merely to obtain finergrained interaction, shifting the optimization focus to generation time rather than chunk duration. 3.2 SPECULATIVE SAMPLING VIA FINITE-STATE MACHINE Our design separates how much the model jointly predicts from how much the system commits at each delivery. Delivery granularity is the number of latents whose pixel frames are transferred together; our method uses = 1, with each regular group spanning δ seconds. For each sampling call, we append 1 noise latents as padding to the next latent to be delivered, forming K-latent bidirectional modeling window. Rather than discarding the resulting padding predictions, we retain them in prediction cache for reuse while the condition remains unchanged. Output commitment makes content non-replaceable and may precede actual playback. large chunk supplies reusable future; the controller keeps that future replaceable until needed. Figure 3 illustrates these actions; Appendix specifies the guards and event updates. 3.3 ADAPTING BIDIRECTIONAL MODELS FOR STREAMING Bidirectional teacher models often define the quality target for causal streaming students, yet their full-sequence generation interfaces are not designed for interactive serving. Directly converting the same backbone to causal generation can also introduce quality gap without careful adaptation (Yin et al., 2024). This motivates further extrapolation of chunk size: can large-chunk bidirectional 5 model itself serve an interactive video stream? We preserve bidirectional joint sampling within each call and adapt its conditioning and output interfaces, allowing successive calls to continue from retained video while outputs are committed incrementally. Continuation interface. Bidirectional video generators commonly provide native imageor video-conditioned continuation interfaces, allowing successive jointly sampled chunks to be connected without modifying within-chunk attention. practical complication arises with temporally compressive 3D VAEs: the continuation interface often expects temporally uncompressed firstframe latent, whereas an interior cached frame belongs to temporally compressed latent group. We therefore decode the retained boundary to pixels and re-encode its final frame through the VAEs first-frame path before the next DiT sampling call. This produces the latent format expected by the pretrained continuation interface. Alternatively, the bidirectional model can be fine-tuned to accept compressed latent continuation directly.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We first characterize how chunk size affects generation quality and computational efficiency within and across GPUs. We then compare conventional chunk commitment and Speculative Sampling in end-to-end interactive serving.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Models and quality evaluation. For Wan1.3B, we follow CF++ (Zhao et al., 2026) and train on Toy6K, {1, 3, 7, 21} models with 1/2/4-step sampling. VBench (Huang et al., 2023) evaluates 81-frame, 16-fps videos at 832 480 and 1280 720 over 946 prompts and five seeds. For LTX2.3 (HaCohen et al., 2026), we train {1, 3, 9, 15, 45} models with three DiT forwards under schedule [999, 757, 522, 0], where 0 is the terminal boundary, on an internal 8K-video training set (Internal8K). We evaluate on an internal 32-case set (Internal32), with matched seeds and 361-frame outputs at 832 448 and 24 fps. We report its six VBench visual scores separately. Forward profiling. We profile Wan with USP over 1/2/4/8 H200 GPUs at batch one and BF16, using shared frame-wise/4-step EMA weights and synthetic inputs with 21-latent prefix plus current latents. We report the slowest-rank median over 30 synchronized forwards after 10 warmups. Timings include forward communication and output gathering but exclude text encoding, VAE decoding, and the sampler loop; these are shape-level profiles rather than generation times C. End-to-end serving protocol. For Wan1.3B, LTX-2.3, and Sol-H3 (NVIDIA, 2026; Li et al., 2026), we compare model-specific small/large chunks under conventional chunk-level commitment (Baseline) or Speculative Sampling. Wan uses K3/USP4 and K21/USP8 on four/eight B300 DiT GPUs, with its real VAE pipelined on separate GPU, at 832 480. LTX uses K3/USP1 with eager or DiT CUDA Graph execution and K15/USP2 with eager execution; all use separate text and media GPUs at 832 448 and 24 fps. Because LTX short eager execution under-runs playback, we also report CUDA Graph variant; the long implementation does not support graph capture, so chunksize comparisons use eager execution. Sol-H3 uses 22and 124-frame proposals with USP4/USP8 on four/eight B300 GPUs at 832 480 and 24 fps. Within each short/long setting, the baseline and our method share model placement, continuation, decoding, playback, and scheduling lead time. Each serving arm receives 30 matched 60-second traces at low (12 updates) and high (311 updates) frequency. Jittered arrivals are independent of playback and vary actions within scene. The baseline applies updates at chunk refills; our method may replace cached suffix. Serving metrics. L50/L95 measure arrival-to-display response after minimum-RTT clock alignment. Across the main short/long comparisons, our method reduces response latency in pattern consistent with the chunk-boundary model. For Sol-H3, the measured short/long mean reductions are 0.493/2.814 s, close to the theoretical 0.438/2.562 s. The gain likewise grows with chunk size for Wan (0.155 to 1.744 s) and LTX eager (0.014 to 2.116 s), matching the predicted trend that larger chunks leave more boundary wait to remove. Large chunks remain responsive and expose serving headroom. Under our method, the longsetting L50 is only 0.260.39 above the corresponding short setting across all three models and both request loads. Meanwhile, long configurations have much lower per-GPU activity for Wan (17 20% versus 5052%) and Sol-H3 (1823% versus 4950%), while LTX eager remains comparable (2125% versus 2223%). This idle time suggests headroom for serving more concurrent streams. Under high-frequency updates, the activity increase over the baseline is somewhat larger, especially for long settings, but long-setting activity remains within 2025%. large chunk can outperform the short baseline. On Sol-H3, the long setting under our method achieves L50 = 1.42/1.41 under low/high update rates, below the short baselines 1.87/1.87 s, with no playback stalls. Thus, retaining larger bidirectional modeling window need not trade away responsiveness.

sections.title: 5 LIMITATIONS AND DISCUSSION
sections.content: The main limitations are twofold. First, our method benefits from predictions only when they are reused before new condition invalidates them; frequent or continuous updates can therefore discard much of each sampled chunk and waste substantial DiT computation. Second, with bidirectional within-chunk attention, the retained KV may encode information from subsequently discarded suffix, so deleting its KV entries may not fully remove its influence on regenerated continuation.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We have formulated interactive video generation as joint problem of prediction and output commitment. Our method preserves multi-latent joint generation, reuses completed predictions under unchanged conditions, and replans only the future that can still be replaced while maintaining feasible playback prefix. This shifts part of the design effort from shrinking the generation unit toward accelerating joint generation, managing revocable predictions, and scheduling timely delivery.

sections.title: D EVENT AND MEASUREMENT SCHEMA
sections.content: Generation is the computation needed to produce deliverable video; its general definition does not require VAE. For the latent diffusion models considered here, includes conditioning preparation, DiT sampling, and required VAE decoding on the critical path to the first output group, not necessarily the entire chunk. Overlapping stages are not simply added. may include scheduling, resource, and conditioning-input readiness waits; may include transport and buffering as well as playback alignment. User-end-to-end latency additionally includes processing before tarrival. Semantic response, when the conditions effect is visibly recognizable, is separate measure. The relation = Kr/f assumes uniform latent-to-frame mapping; models with nonuniform mappings or overlap trimming use their actual output frame counts. The temporal frame rate is not computational throughput in generated frames per wall-clock second. Each event log should include run identifier, event identifier, condition version, condition-ready time, prefix-ready time, generation start, KV-ready time, DiT sampling completion, VAE decoding completion, first deliverable output time, target switch boundary, actual display time, and final outcome. Generation logs additionally record call identifier, absolute positions, used and discarded predictions, runtime, GPU count, and any canceled or repeated work. Model, DiT sampling, resolution, frame-rate, and buffer configurations belong in run metadata. Record the conditioning adapter, retained-context identity, source-to-playback offsets, and trimmed overlap, so native image continuation is not conflated with retained-prefix KV reuse. Use identical external event streams for paired policy comparisons. Report the randomization of wall-clock arrival phases and do not restrict events to convenient generation boundaries. Repeated16 run uncertainty should be estimated at the run or paired-run level when events within rollout are dependent. Record the warm-up and final-buffer accounting policy.

sections.title: E CONDITIONING AND OUTPUT ADAPTERS
sections.content: The controller operates on retained content and playback deadlines. Its conditioning state Hj need not have the same representation across generators. This section distinguishes the adapters used to expose continuation, rather than treating all streaming paths as full-prefix KV reuse. Retained-prefix KV. For generator with history-conditioned DiT sampling, the adapter exposes the selected prefixs inference state at the correct positions. Direct suffix entries are invalidated while the retained KV is reused. This preserves the original inference representations; it does not reconstruct them from clean latents. An implementation that instead builds KV by clean prefill of each retained latent is different cache policy. An LTX proposal-reuse implementation may instead use incremental clean prefill; that should be identified separately from direct retained-KV reuse. Neither policy can erase old-future information already present in fixed prefix latent values. Separating the additional effect of KV reuse requires matched controlled ablation. Boundary-image continuation. The bidirectional image-conditioned path retrieves the fullresolution RGB frame immediately preceding the selected branch from the retained timeline, then submits it through the checkpoints native image conditioning interface with the latest available prompt. The H3 image-conditioned path can implement this operation without new temporal causal mask or wrapper-specific training. This path conditions on the boundary image rather than full-prefix KV or equivalent long-range context. Latent and multi-frame variants. The H3 experimental latent-input path replaces image encoding with normalized clean video latent while retaining condition packing and condition-noise handling. This differs from copying the latent into the target noise tensor, and its conditioning distribution differs from that of single encoded image. separate multi-frame path supplies phase-aligned group of retained latents as keyframe conditions and removes the corresponding output overlap. These variants change context, eligible boundaries, and preparation costs, and are reported separately from the boundary-image adapter. Output mapping and VAE state. native clip may include regenerated anchor or context span. The output adapter omits that span and maps only the remaining pixels to the new playback interval. It retains source indices for subsequent anchors, and never selects history from discarded or trimmed-away prediction. This mapping can have nonuniform latent-to-frame spans and fewer playable groups than sampled latents; the controller uses their actual deadlines. Streaming VAE decoding can publish finalized groups before the entire clip has finished decoding, while DiT sampling remains joint over the chunk. This does not imply that prefix of bidirectional DiT sampling is available early. VAE overlap and any state dependent on replaced suffix must be handled before pixels are committed; the adapter may instead decode the full clip and deliver its completed frames incrementally. Group-ready and job-finish events remain separate in both cases. History encoding, cache construction, VAE decoding, and mandatory overlap work are included in the corresponding timing and cost measurements. FUTURE WORK: CO-OPTIMIZING DIT SAMPLING AND VAE DECODING Accelerating joint DiT sampling is one route to retaining large chunks, but the serving objective is to reduce generation time to the first deliverable output group. natural next step is to codesign DiT sampling and VAE decoding as single generation pipeline rather than optimize their isolated runtimes. This includes when completed latent groups are handed to the VAE decoder, how decoding is scheduled against playback deadlines, and how compute and memory are allocated between stages. Overlap schedules must respect the data dependencies of temporally bidirectional DiT sampling and VAE decoding. Candidate schedules should measure time to the first deliverable group, later-group 17 deadlines, total GPU cost, and playback stalls. Parallel acceleration should be evaluated within the complete pipeline and resource budget.
